cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-149-chris.summary: On an eminence at the right stands the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, attended by saints, while women with harps and drums sing and dance before him. Below, saints with 'the high praises of God in their mouth, and a two-edged sword in their hand' stand in a building, and captured kings are led in chains or sit in the stocks: 'to bind their kings with chains'. It is the upper drawing of folio 83r.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
The psalter was made in or near Reims, probably under Archbishop Ebbo (816–835); some scholars argue for a date around 850 under his successor Hincmar.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-149-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-healing-leper.summary: Accompanied by three apostles, Christ reaches out to a leper whose body is covered with spots and who has a horn slung on his back. Below, in a separate scene framed by twin towers and arches, a young man stands before a seated, haloed elder — probably the cleansed leper presenting himself as Christ commanded.
facts: The Gospels of Otto III has 276 leaves, twelve canon tables, a double-page portrait of the emperor, four evangelist portraits and 29 full-page miniatures of New Testament scenes; it was produced at Reichenau around 1000.
Its original cover still holds a 10th-century Byzantine ivory of the Dormition of the Virgin.
cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-healing-leper.notes: The lower scene is not securely identified; Christ appears only in the upper register. Folio derived from the BSB image sequence (image 198); verify against the foliation on the page.

cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-bartimaeus.summary: Before a domed city gate, Christ reaches out toward the blind beggar Bartimaeus, who sits on the ground with his staff and begging bowl and raises his hands; apostles stand behind Christ and the people of Jericho on the right. The Index of Medieval Art catalogues the page as fol. 119r.
facts: The Gospels of Otto III has 276 leaves, twelve canon tables, a double-page portrait of the emperor, four evangelist portraits and 29 full-page miniatures of New Testament scenes; it was produced at Reichenau around 1000.
The Bayerische Staatsbibliothek has published the whole manuscript online with a Public Domain Mark, so every page can be studied in detail.
cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-bartimaeus.notes: Folio derived from the BSB image sequence (image 241); verify against the foliation on the page.

cur:monumental-san-led-to-calvary.summary: The bearded Christ, haloed and robed in purple, is led forward by a soldier in a blue tunic, while Simon of Cyrene, in red, carries the long cross beside him. In keeping with Early Christian reticence, the cycle passes from this scene directly to the empty tomb, without showing the Crucifixion itself.
facts: On the south wall the thirteen Passion and Resurrection scenes show Christ bearded; the cycle omits both the Flagellation and the Crucifixion.
The scenes were not arranged in biblical order but are thought to follow the Gospel readings of the Lenten liturgy in Theodoric's palace church.

walters:W.185.58V.summary: Christ stands bound to a slender pink column, naked except for a loincloth, his body marked with wounds. Two tormentors in brightly coloured tunics and hose lunge at him from either side with raised scourges, their twisting poses contrasting with his stillness. The black-and-white chequered floor and patterned gold ground give the small scene a jewel-like intensity.
facts: The book is named after Franchoise de Doffinnes, who owned it in the late 16th century; her family's later history is recorded on its final folios.

Its calendar follows the Use of Utrecht and its Hours of the Virgin largely the Use of the Windesheim Congregation, pointing to a Dutch origin; it contains both Latin and Dutch texts and twelve full-page miniatures by the Master of Walters 185.
walters:W.185.58V.notes: Museum date (1400–1425) applies to the whole Book of Hours; the date in our data (8th century) was an import error.
